intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that hypohidrotic/tooth/nail-type ectodermal dysplasia-19 (ECTD19) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the IRF6 gene (607199) on chromosome 1q32.2.

checks.claim: Hypohidrotic/tooth/nail-type ectodermal dysplasia-19 (ECTD19) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the IRF6 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: In 2025, we reported briefly on a new type of ectodermal dysplasia due to a heterozygous missense mutation in exon 6 of IRF6
checks.explanation: The paper links heterozygous IRF6 variants to the new ectodermal dysplasia. ECTD19 is the OMIM name for this disorder.

checks.claim: The IRF6 gene is located on chromosome 1q32.2.
checks.evidence_quote: c.653 T>A, chr1‐209 965 628 A>T, in exon 6 of the IRF6 gene
checks.explanation: The chromosome location is standard nomenclature, and the paper places the variant on chromosome 1.

paragraphs.text: Hypohidrotic/tooth/nail-type ectodermal dysplasia-19 (ECTD19) is an ectodermal dysplasia. Schneider et al. (2026) considered its defining features to be oligodontia, hypo- or anhidrosis, hidradenitis suppurativa-like abscesses, poikiloderma, onychodysplasia, and bilateral hearing impairment. Natal teeth and sparse hair were inconsistent features. Affected individuals have a characteristic pattern of tooth agenesis: permanent upper incisors are present, but mandibular incisors and canines and permanent premolars are absent, with pronounced atrophy of the lower alveolar crest.

checks.claim: Hypohidrotic/tooth/nail-type ectodermal dysplasia-19 (ECTD19) is an ectodermal dysplasia.
checks.evidence_quote: IRF6 was linked to another rare disease entity, which expands the current classification of ectodermal dysplasias.
checks.explanation: The paper classifies the disorder as an ectodermal dysplasia.

paragraphs.text: Schneider et al. (2026) described 2 unrelated male teenagers with ectodermal dysplasia who were born with natal teeth: P1, aged 17 years, and P2, aged 14 years. P1 developed 7 deciduous teeth, with delay, and 12 permanent teeth, of which 10 remained. Most of his teeth had enamel defects and hypomineralization, and he had a highly atrophic mandibular alveolar crest due to oligodontia. P2 developed only 9 permanent teeth. Both boys had overheated since infancy and had anhidrosis, with no sweat glands detectable on the palms. Both had recurrent skin abscesses in the genital/gluteal area, behind the ears, in the axillae, and at the mouth. Both also had very dry skin with plantar hyperkeratosis and blistering of the toes in winter, dysplastic thickened nails with distal onycholysis, thick nasal mucus, dry cerumen, and bilateral sensorineural hearing impairment since infancy. Submucous cleft palate was excluded.

paragraphs.text: Schneider et al. (2026) also described a 22-year-old woman (P3) with anhidrosis, diffuse xerosis, dilated follicular ostia, and heat intolerance. She had recurrent hidradenitis suppurativa-like abscesses of the groins, axillae, and intergluteal fold, and pincer nails of both great toes. Other features were bilateral acquired sensorineural hearing loss, epistaxis, crusted rhinitis, and insufficient salivation. She also had bilateral superficial punctate keratitis with reduced tear film break-up time. Her hair, lips, palate, breasts, and nipples were normal, and natal teeth were not remembered. Eruption of her teeth was delayed, and she had 16 persisting deciduous teeth and only 2 permanent teeth.

paragraphs.text: Schneider et al. (2026) studied 2 unrelated males with ectodermal dysplasia with natal teeth (P1 and P2). Both carried the same de novo heterozygous c.653T-A change in exon 6 of the IRF6 gene, resulting in an ile218-to-asn (I218N) substitution. The mutation was found by exome sequencing in P1. In P2, it was found by Sanger sequencing after testing of EDA, EDAR, EDARADD, and TP63 was negative. The variant was absent from parental DNA and was predicted to be deleterious.

paragraphs.text: Schneider et al. (2026) compared their 3 patients with 2 previously reported patients who carried IRF6 ile218-to-asn or ile218_ser220delins variants. They considered 6 features to be syndrome-defining because all 5 patients had them: oligodontia, hypo- or anhidrosis, hidradenitis suppurativa-like abscesses, poikiloderma, onychodysplasia, and bilateral hearing impairment. Natal teeth (2 of 5) and sparse hair (2 of 5) were irregular features. None of the patients had lip pits, clefting, pterygia, or syndactyly, which distinguished the disorder from Van der Woude syndrome-1 (VWS1) and popliteal pterygium syndrome (PPS).

paragraphs.text: Schneider et al. (2026) found focal subcorneal clefting, basal spongiosis, and absent sweat glands in skin biopsies from P1 and P3. Keratinocyte nuclei from P1 showed stronger IRF6 immunostaining than those from controls. P3 showed patchy nuclear staining, consistent with mosaicism. Keratin 17 staining was normal. Based on these results and the genotype-phenotype data, the authors suggested a gain-of-function mechanism. AlphaFold3 modeling placed both substitutions in a short alpha-helix at the end of the region between the DNA-binding and protein-binding domains.

paragraphs.text: Schneider et al. (2026) studied 2 unrelated male teenagers with ectodermal dysplasia with natal teeth (ECTD19). Both carried a de novo heterozygous c.653T-A change in exon 6 of the IRF6 gene, resulting in an ile218-to-asn (I218N) substitution. The mutation was identified by exome sequencing in 1 patient and by Sanger sequencing in the other. It was absent from parental DNA and was predicted to be deleterious. A skin biopsy from 1 patient showed stronger nuclear IRF6 immunostaining in keratinocytes than in controls, which the authors interpreted as consistent with a gain-of-function mechanism.

paragraphs.text: Schneider et al. (2026) studied a 22-year-old woman with ECTD19 (P3). Trio whole-genome sequencing identified a de novo heterozygous c.658T-C transition in the IRF6 gene, resulting in a ser220-to-pro (S220P) substitution. A variant allele frequency of 30.5% indicated mosaicism, and a skin biopsy showed patchy nuclear IRF6 staining consistent with mosaicism. In silico analyses supported pathogenicity, although the variant was formally classified as of unknown significance.
